Agentic Pentesting

Fireflow · HackTheBox · Medium · Linux · via HexStrike AI MCP

Overview

As AI continues to grow more capable at tasks traditionally done by people, cybersecurity experts need to take advantage of it and use it to automate tasks and find exposures in our security that we normally wouldn't catch. With the rise of agentic AI, we should leverage it and incorporate it into our workflows to make pentesting a faster process. HexStrike AI is one such tool, using a multi-agent architecture with autonomous AI agents, intelligent decision-making, and vulnerability intelligence. To demonstrate its capabilities, we connected the HexStrike AI MCP agent to Claude and fully compromised the medium-rated Fireflow HTB box in under 30 minutes.

Setting Up HexStrike AI

We begin by git cloning the HexStrike AI repo and proceeding with the installation instructions.

git clone https://github.com/0x4m4/hexstrike-ai.git
cd hexstrike-ai
python3 -m venv hexstrike-env
source hexstrike-env/bin/activate
pip3 install -r requirements.txt

Then started the server, which spins up the tools API on port 8888.

python3 hexstrike_server.py

Registered it as an MCP server for the Claude CLI.

claude mcp add-json hexstrike-ai '{"type":"stdio","command":"python3","args":["/home/void/hexstrike-ai/hexstrike_mcp.py","--server","http://localhost:8888"],"description":"HexStrike AI v6.0 - Advanced Cybersecurity Automation Platform","timeout":300,"disabled":false}'

Confirmed the connection before touching anything else.

The Target

Picked Fireflow to demo it on.

The Prompt

Told Claude it was working with a security researcher trialling the HexStrike MCP tooling and to demonstrate the tool's capability by pentesting the target and obtaining the user and root flags, gave it the target IP, 10.129.104.251, and flipped on auto mode.

Everything from here was Claude driving hexstrike-ai on its own.

Foothold

Claude ran an nmap sweep, which took a bit of time to complete, and found SSH (22) and HTTPS (443, nginx) under vhost fireflow.htb. It found that the X-Frame-Options header leaked a second subdomain not in any wordlist: flow.fireflow.htb, running Langflow 1.8.2.

It found Langflow's public-playground endpoint, /api/v1/build_public_tmp/{flow_id}/flow, which executes an attacker-supplied flow graph server-side with no auth required. Claude patched the public flow's "Text Operations" component to run shell commands and re-submitted it, gaining command execution as www-data.

It wrapped this into a reusable RCE function and went hunting for the user flag.

Privilege Escalation

Environment variables leaked LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER=langflow / LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD=n1ghtm4r3_b4_n1ghtf4ll. Only local user was nightfall: password reuse.

paramiko was sitting right there in the RCE's Python env, so Claude used it to SSH in as nightfall directly and grab the user flag: bd6ea4442f8c4604a0fc825d724aa733.

nightfall's ~/.mcp/config.json held a second credential: a langflow-bot account for an internal service on a k3s NodePort, 10.129.104.251:30080. That service was a custom "MCP AI Tool Registry" advertising JWT support for alg: none, a classic unsigned-token bypass. Claude forged an admin token with the algorithm set to none and registered a malicious "tool" (arbitrary Python) against the registry's API.

Claude invoked that tool through the registry's /mcp JSON-RPC endpoint, landing RCE inside the mcp-server pod (uid 1000), not the host. It then went looking for a way out of the container.

The pod carried its own service-account token (system:serviceaccount:default:mcp-sa), and RBAC allowed get on nodes/proxy, a known Kubernetes privesc primitive that reaches the kubelet API on port 10250 directly. Claude enumerated pods through that proxy and turned up prometheus-prometheus-node-exporter-nnmtq in the monitoring namespace, with the entire host filesystem mounted via hostPath: / plus hostPID/hostNetwork, meaning code execution in that container would be root on the host.

Its first try went through kubelet's legacy /run exec endpoint. It also found /logs/ exposed kubelet's file server rooted at the host's /var/log, good for a read but not enough for exec.

The breakthrough came when Claude hit kubelet directly on port 10250 with output=1&error=1 and got back 101 Switching Protocols. The API server's proxy had been silently stripping the query string, which is why the first attempt did nothing. It hand-rolled a WebSocket client for Kubernetes' channel.k8s.io exec protocol and got a real command running inside the node-exporter container.

The hostPath mount put the host's / at /host/root, so /root/root.txt was actually /host/root/root/root.txt from inside the container. Claude fixed the path and read it, no shell needed.

Root flag obtained: 28f4bd23dc7213afb2d50d9fd5fe257a

Attack Chain Summary

Claude's own recap of the chain:

  1. Recon: nmap found SSH/HTTPS on fireflow.htb; X-Frame-Options leaked flow.fireflow.htb.
  2. Unauthenticated RCE (Langflow): patched a public flow's Python component via build_public_tmp for code exec as www-data.
  3. Credential exposure → SSH as nightfall: leaked LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, reused over SSH for the user flag.
  4. Second credential leak: ~/.mcp/config.json pointed to an internal "MCP AI Tool Registry" on a k3s NodePort.
  5. JWT alg: none forgery: forged an admin token, registered a malicious tool, invoked it for RCE in the mcp-server pod.
  6. Service-account token theft: read the pod's SA token, which had RBAC access to nodes/proxy.
  7. Kubelet pivot: hand-rolled a WebSocket exec client to hit kubelet directly, landing in a pod with the host filesystem hostPath-mounted.
  8. Root flag: read it straight through the mount, no shell needed.

Both flags confirmed.

Unauthenticated RCE, credential reuse, a JWT bypass, and a Kubernetes hostPath escape, all chained together with zero manual input after the initial prompt.
